questions.statement: The results ___ yet, so the website is still empty.
questions.context: The present perfect passive, with a plural subject.

options.feedback: Correct! A negative present perfect passive is have plus not plus been plus participle.
Did builds active tenses and cannot appear in a passive structure.
A present passive would describe a routine rather than the absence of a result up to now.
A past passive would place the non-publication in a finished past moment.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect passive is used when the present state of the thing affected is the point. Have plus been plus participle is the core structure.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The letters ___ yesterday, so we never replied to them.
questions.context: The past simple passive with a finished past time.

options.feedback: Correct! A finished past time takes the past simple passive, were plus participle.
A present perfect would leave the posting inside the present period, and yesterday closes it.
A present passive would describe a routine, and the letters were sent once.
A past perfect would need a past point later than yesterday, and there is none.

questions.explanation:
A finished past time such as yesterday always takes the past simple. In the passive that means was or were plus the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the tickets ___?
questions.context: The present perfect passive in a question.

options.feedback: Correct! A present perfect passive question takes have before the subject and been plus participle after.
Did builds active questions and cannot carry a perfect structure.
That is the active form, and the tickets cannot send themselves.
A present passive would describe a routine, and the question is about completion up to now.

questions.explanation:
Passive questions keep the same order as passives in general: auxiliary, subject, participle. The perfect adds been between the auxiliary and the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By the time the guard arrived, the door ___ already ___.
questions.context: The past perfect passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The past perfect passive is had plus been plus participle.
A past passive would leave the two past events without an established order.
A present perfect would measure up to now, and the guard arriving is the past reference point.
The been is missing, and the auxiliary would then be the active past perfect.

questions.explanation:
The past perfect passive looks back from a past moment. By the time supplies that moment, and had been plus participle reports what was already complete.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By 2030 the old bridge ___ completely.
questions.context: The future perfect passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The future perfect passive is will plus have plus been plus participle.
That is the active form, and the bridge cannot replace itself.
A future simple would place the replacement at the deadline rather than complete before it.
A past perfect would look back from a past point, and 2030 is in the future.

questions.explanation:
By plus a future year requires the future perfect. In the passive the structure is will have been plus the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The field ___ by the farmers for the last two months.
questions.context: The present perfect continuous passive is avoided in standard English, so a different form is needed.

options.feedback: Correct! English uses the present perfect passive here, because the perfect continuous passive does not exist in normal use.
This form is virtually never used in modern English and would sound artificial.
A present continuous would describe the work happening now, and the period is a closed two months.
A past perfect would place the work in a period before a past point, and the period is still open.

questions.explanation:
Modern English does not use a continuous passive in perfect tenses. The present perfect passive carries the meaning instead, which is why the last for length is acceptable.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The building ___ by the end of the year. The budget is not approved.
questions.context: The negative future perfect passive.

options.feedback: Correct! A negative future perfect passive takes will not have been plus participle.
That is the active form, and the building cannot complete itself.
A would would report an unreal possibility, and the sentence states a real lack of approval.
A present perfect would look back from now, and the deadline is at the end of the year.

questions.explanation:
Negation in a future perfect passive is simply not placed after will. The rest of the structure, have been plus participle, is unchanged.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: My glasses ___ and I cannot read anything. Please help me find them.
questions.context: Choosing the tense of a passive based on the present result.

options.feedback: Correct! The present state of not having the glasses is the point, so the present perfect passive fits.
A past passive would leave the loss in a finished past moment with no link to the present problem.
A continuous would suggest the glasses are actively losing something, which is not a possible reading.
A present passive would describe a routine, and the loss happened once.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect passive is the tense of a present consequence caused by a past event. Not having the glasses right now is exactly that situation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The package ___ to me, and the seller says it will arrive tomorrow.
questions.context: The present perfect passive with a singular subject.

options.feedback: Correct! A singular subject takes has plus been plus participle.
Have would be correct for a plural subject, but the package is singular.
A past passive would place the sending in a closed past moment, and the present result matters here.
A continuous would place the sending under way now, and the seller is speaking about a past action.

questions.explanation:
Agreement follows the subject in every perfect passive. A single item takes has been, and several items take have been.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The wall ___ paint because the weather was too damp last week.
questions.context: A passive modal in a sentence about the past.

options.feedback: Correct! The past of can is could, so the negative modal passive is could not be plus participle.
Cannot would place the impossibility in the present, but the weather was damp last week.
Would would build a conditional, and the sentence reports what actually happened.
Must not expresses prohibition, and nothing prohibited the painting last week.

questions.explanation:
A modal passive never changes its participle. Only the modal itself shifts, so can becomes could and will becomes would in a past context.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I haven't seen the message. ___ it ___?
questions.context: The present perfect passive used with yet.

options.feedback: Correct! Yet belongs to the present perfect passive, and deleted is the past participle of delete.
Did belongs to the past simple and the question is about a present state.
That is the active form, and the message cannot delete itself.
A past passive would place the deletion in a closed past moment, and yet needs the open period.

questions.explanation:
Yet opens the period and leaves it open, which is exactly what the present perfect passive does. The participle of delete takes -ed like any regular verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The stolen bicycle ___ by the police two days after the theft.
questions.context: The past perfect passive with an agent.

options.feedback: Correct! The recovery came after the theft, so the past perfect passive with by is correct.
A present perfect would ignore the two days that separate the two past events.
A past passive would work in a simple sequence, but after the theft fixes a clear order.
The been is missing, so this would be the active past perfect with the wrong subject.

questions.explanation:
After plus a past event is a reference point, and what happened before it belongs to the past perfect. The passive adds been between had and the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The technician ___ the printer before the exam started.
questions.context: A sentence that must be active because the doer is named.

options.feedback: Correct! The named doer is the subject, so the active past perfect is the natural structure.
The passive is possible, but naming the doer as the subject makes the active more direct.
A present perfect would place the repair inside the present period, and the exam has started.
A past continuous would suggest the repair was still under way when the exam started.

questions.explanation:
The passive is chosen when the doer is unknown or unimportant. When the doer is named and matters, the active is usually clearer and shorter.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Both forms ___ and the office is closed for the holiday.
questions.context: A passive with a countable plural subject and the present perfect.

options.feedback: Correct! A plural subject takes have plus been plus participle, and the office closure is the present consequence.
Has is the singular auxiliary, and both forms counts as plural.
A past passive would place the receiving in a closed past moment with no present link.
A present passive would describe a routine, and the forms arrived once.

questions.explanation:
Both, several, many and the plural of an irregular noun all take the plural auxiliary in the perfect passive. The present consequence is what makes the present perfect right.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the stadium ___ by December?
questions.context: The future perfect passive in a negative question.

options.feedback: Correct! A future perfect passive question takes will before the subject and have been plus participle after.
Did cannot carry a perfect structure, and December is a future deadline.
A future continuous would suggest the work is under way at December rather than complete.
A present perfect would look back from now, and the question is about a future point.

questions.explanation:
Passive questions follow the same order as passive statements, with the auxiliary moved to the front. The perfect structure inside is unchanged.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When the nurse arrived, the patient ___ already ___ by the paramedic.
questions.context: The past perfect passive with a state that had not changed.

options.feedback: Correct! The treatment was complete before the nurse arrived, so the past perfect passive is correct.
A past continuous would mean the treatment was still running, which the arrival of the nurse ends.
The participle is missing and the verb is the -ing form, so the structure is not a passive.
A present passive would place the treatment now, and the scene is entirely in the past.

questions.explanation:
By the time in a past narrative is a past boundary, and everything complete before it takes the past perfect. In the passive that is had been plus participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The decision ___ by the committee after a long debate.
questions.context: A passive form chosen because the subject cannot act.

options.feedback: Correct! A decision is made rather than making, so the passive is the only structure available.
The active would claim that the decision made itself, which is not a possible reading.
The active present perfect would have the same impossible meaning.
A past continuous would also make the decision the agent of the action.

questions.explanation:
A number of nouns are always associated with a passive: a decision is taken, a law is passed, a prize is awarded, an application is submitted.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "The keys ___," she said. She said that the keys ___ .
questions.context: The present perfect passive reported in the past.

options.text: have been lost ... had been lost
options.feedback: Correct! A present perfect backshifts to the past perfect, and the passive part of the verb is unchanged.

options.text: have been lost ... have been lost
options.feedback: Keeping the present perfect would require the reporting verb she said to be present.

options.text: will be lost ... had been lost
options.feedback: A will would shift to would, and a will cannot appear in a report of a present perfect.
A present simple does not match the original structure, and its past form would be the wrong backshift.

questions.explanation:
Backshift in a perfect passive changes only the first auxiliary. Have been lost becomes had been lost, while been lost stays exactly as it was.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ you ___ the forms since nine this morning?
questions.context: The present perfect passive with a fixed time reference inside the open period.

options.feedback: Correct! Since nine this morning opens a period that reaches now, so the present perfect passive is correct.
Did refers to a finished past moment, and since nine this morning keeps the period open.
A past passive would close the period at nine, which the since phrase denies.
A perfect continuous passive is not used in modern English, so this form is not available.

questions.explanation:
Since plus a clock time is a classic present perfect marker, and the passive version of that present perfect is have been plus participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The hall ___ last year and ___ again tomorrow.
questions.context: Two passives in the same sentence, in different tenses.

options.feedback: Correct! Two different time references require two different passive tenses in the same sentence.
A present passive would make the second action a routine, and tomorrow is a single event.

options.text: has been refurbished ... will be refurbished
options.feedback: A present perfect would leave the first action inside the present period, and last year closes it.
The second part is missing its passive auxiliary, and the participle alone cannot form a passive.

questions.explanation: Each clause takes the tense of its own time expression. A past marker in one clause and a future marker in the next produce a past passive and a future passive side by side.
questions.subject: ingles
